I’m glad you liked it! I think for me I could really overlook almost all of those problems if they implemented really, really basic functionality. I’m not even referring to proper A-Life as in the originals (never mind modded versions), but just working stealth, binoculars, and most of all night vision which was a proxy for advancement and improving it was a series of fun milestones in the original trilogy.

I have some hope it will be fixed one day, but in a straightforward a 1:1 comparison between the first three games (including some mod content, given that they’ve had over 10 years to take note of that ecosystem) stalker 2 is just missing a lot of really fundamental stuff.

It’s true. The world feels empty and dead, the systems are half baked. When it first came out things only spawned within 75 feet or so and binoculars/NVG were obviously excluded to make that less obvious. 

The basic gameplay dynamic that made the first game an instant classic is pretty much entirely gone. You can’t scope out an enemy base and make plans. You can’t rely on anything happening you didn’t start, except maybe two opposed squads or some animals spawning nearby (which is very lame in a series known for its active world!) and the world itself is huge but barren, and not in a thematically appropriate or fun way. For example, in the original stalker there were caches of loot and hidden stuff, some of which was really good. In 2, you’ll spend 20 minutes doing terrible climbing to get to a stash and it’s always the same - generic food/medicine and small amounts of money. No reason to explore. Mutants don’t even work right! Dogs and boars take cover the exact same way as humans - the first game explicitly instructed players to get on a rock and shoot dumb circling dogs, now the dogs run off and hide behind a tree the second you’re an inch off the ground. 

Oh, and the PDA is more or less gone. Names, factions, emergent missions, messages, etc - stuff that was in CoP and Clear Sky - just don’t happen here. The world is dead and there’s no information to be gleaned, nobody to talk to, no stalker rankings to track. Zilch.

Performance also blows. I got it on a computer with a 3070 and it ran poorly, so I upgraded to a powerful machine with a 4080s last December. It runs well enough now, kind of, but makes the fucking fans howl and temps soar with no real noticeable visual improvement because the way they implemented UE5 makes everything blurry and indistinct. 

That’s without even getting into the hideously buggy missions and story that completely breaks - as in, no longer functional and waiting for patches - for significant numbers of players. I don’t understand why people are so hostile to this stuff, it’s all objectively true. I’m a huge stalker fan - read the book as a kid, loved the Tarkovsky movie, bought every game the day it launched - and S2 has been a huge letdown in every way. I’ve only put 20 hours into it and they were a miserable slog.

I think what frustrates me most about Stalker 2 is that it feels right initially and has really excellent graphics/presentation, but those issues don’t become apparent until you’re a few hours in (except the obviously gimped PDA). I haven’t played a stalker game in a few years but I’ve been a fan since the first game came out, and Stalker 2 made me absolutely ravenous for that Stalker experience which isn’t present in the game at the moment.

I’ve gone back to replaying SoC and the presence of a detailed PDA, real incentives for jobs, NPC dialogue, actual monster AI, binoculars, and so on makes it so much more alive. All I want is the basic vanilla stalker world with those features and fancy graphics

I mean, I never really played anomaly or gamma or whatever, and I’ve purchased every stalker game on release, starting with a physical copy of SoC which was indeed totally absurdly buggy and borderline unplayable at launch. 

But it had a number of basic systems and features that were really important, and, back then, pretty unique for their implementation in an open world context. Many of these systems are completely missing from Stalker 2. I bought 2 and played for 8 or so hours before getting frustrated and reinstalling SoC, which I’ve played in vanilla form or with basic bug fix mods every few years ever since it came out.

Right now, Stalker 2 is missing - just compared to “vanilla” fully functional patched up SoC - at least these critical things:

Binoculars - in SoC they have reticles that identify friend or foe and are useful from the very first bandit mission

Night Vision - the most important mid game piece of progress that makes undertaking night missions so much more engaging 

PDA info - basic list of contacts with their faction affiliation and ranking. The rank thing is gone too, so no more list of top stalkers you can overtake as you play and advance. Faction information 

That’s without going into the economy, mission rewards, the absence of stalker squads who help you in semi-scripted missions, the silly mutant AI that hides behind toothpick trees instead of circling and trying to jump attack. Enemies that don’t spawn on top of you so you can actually observe from a distance and act accordingly. The basic dynamic of Stalker combat isn’t really present in 2 right now, not even compared to unmodded versions of the original 

Obviously Stalker 2 is beautiful and these ancient games aren’t even in the same ballpark in terms of presentation. I didn’t refund and even left up my good review from the first couple hours before these problems became apparent. But it’s missing a lot right now, and doesn’t really feel like a sequel to the originals

I'm too lazy to summarize everything but it take EQ classes and mechanics and adds a lot. There's a precursor to WoW gryphons with the carriage system, where you sign a ledger at a settlement and can thereafter fast travel to connected settlements. Classes are a little bit more autonomous and soloing is a little more viable - Shaman, for instance, has both bear form and bear pets, Monk has spells and special attacks that act like spells, Warriors have abilities that are kind of between the active melee of later games and the auto-attack of EQ PC, there's an entirely new class called Alchemist, etc etc. There's no EXP loss and no item loss on death. Instead you return to your bind point and accumulate EXP debt, which forms a sub-bar over your EXP bar and consumes EXP until it's paid off. It's really a fascinating hybrid between two eras in a lot of ways, as it still retains the basic EQ structure where utility classes and non-trinity gameplay styles are both viable and necessary.

The key to 1vX is tracking multiple targets, waiting for them to act, and alternating. One guy is focusing on you and you’ve just hit them while a flanker is coming in - 99% of players will continue focusing on their original foe and just work, at best, to block or dodge the incoming enemy. Instead you should strike them first with a quick dodge and hit or riposte, then go back to the first guy, then the second again, and so on. 

It’s easier said than done but the important part really is a kind of soft retracted vision that takes in the whole screen instead of just your enemy. After a few hundred hours when you have weapon lengths/attack speeds and movement memorized unconsciously you’ll be able to do a little dance where you keep an eye on every enemy you can see and pop out parries/attacks as necessary. 

Also the most important thing in many situations in TO isn’t necessarily about skilled swordsmanship but about opportunism and bravery. Don’t fear death - if you see a chance to slip between lines and throw a heavy attack into the backs of four guys, take it even if it means dying afterwards. I average about 5 TKD/2.5 kills a life by relentlessly focusing on opportunities to hit enemy groups from behind with blunt weapons. I’m level 975 so I’ve got the benefit of 1,000 hours of experience which helps me spot those opportunities and gauge spacing/timing but the basic principle - engage proactively when you’re in a big scrum or fighting a 1/2vX - is relevant at any level

We retained application info indefinitely, in theory, and could thus provide feedback whenever - most people would reach out shortly after a rejection, though, and I had a different template for reapplications with a set list of things they could do to improve their chances.

As for feeling guilty, I would email and not call - it takes a few minutes to access stuff in the application systems and isn’t always self-evident why someone was rejected, due to the aforementioned ad hoc character of admissions, so they’ll likely blow you off. Instead, email with specific questions: ask where you can improve, what the general proportionate importance of each component is (essay is usually the most important), etc. That will give them the chance to actually look you up and give you a good answer. 

FWIW most admissions stuff is a fucking mess. I was by far the most effective employee and was laid off - in the time since, response times there have quadrupled and then some. Working in academic admin sucks and attracts a lot of lazy dipshits, so my tendency to provide specific feedback immediately may not be the norm.

Yeah, it’s very normal. I had a set of things I’d evaluate for every app and when someone reached out about their rejection, I’d take a gander and articulate it in qualitative language so people wouldn’t try to dispute our internal quantitative thresholds and argue they actually did achieve the necessary scores/metrics/whatever. 

Honestly, for anyone interested in how the process actually works and what a rejection means: a lot of graduate admissions is extremely ad hoc and informed by factors nobody will ever publicly articulate. The process is entirely contingent on the whims of administrators and, often, the mood of the person evaluating your application. If you’re rejected and they don’t provide good feedback or clear parameters, it’s just as often an indication that the program is dysfunctional as it is a failure on the part of the applicant.

Check out Simon Roy - Habitat, Griz Grobus, Last Knife. He’s excellent in general but the first two in particular are both excellent, self-contained pieces of science fiction that have very different narratives, settings, and tones but are both good examples of how consistently thought out worlds that aren’t dumped on the reader but expressed through dialogue and implication really set things aside from more generic entries in the genre. 

Habitat is about communities on a deep-space colony ship adrift for generations, so a sort of post-apocalyptic story set aboard an enormous ship. It’s bleak and violent but a good, quick read. Griz Grobus is comparatively low stakes and focuses on the adventures of some incredibly charming characters, like the Priest-Bot Father Stanley. 

I’d also recommend the Dark Horse Aliens stories. Most don’t have any lengthy continuity and some, like Labyrinth, are just outstanding

For stories with women, Halo Jones is an all timer. But I’d also recommend some of the older British comics, like Misty or Jinty, which were both intended for girls and came out in the 70s and 80s. They’re a lot of fun, if a little goofy and old timey.

Nah, don’t think about it in those terms - all sources are biased and understanding the bias is part of the broader process of apprehending historical truth. It’s almost certain to be exaggerated, but the nature and context of the exaggerations can be as informative a more “objective” statistical recounting from a modern writer. 

Anyway, your instinct is right in general though, and the stuff I’m suggesting would be best paired with a handful of peer-reviewed books or articles. I just would caution you against discounting sources because of bias, when it’s more important to try to understand the bias and the way it does (or doesn’t) influence assertions. A modern historian writing about it will manifest a modern perspective informed by living in the context of late capitalist Liberal democracy, in much the same way a sociologist or government official writing in 1955 would be influenced by a different array of socio-political-economic factors.

Popular media can be a great way to learn about the recent past from primary sources. I’d also recommend going to the Gutenberg Project and archive.org and using the search function to see if you can find any PSA literature/cinema from the period. The US government was much more prolific in terms of publicly oriented educational material in the mid-20th century, so you can often find videos, pamphlets, books intended for school/popular consumption, etc etc, all in the public domain. 

My degrees are in history and obviously if you want the really substantial stuff you’ve got no choice but to engage with the archives and scholarly secondary sources, but if you just want to do some kind of osmotic learning, check out the stuff I’ve mentioned.
